title: Routing, switching, BGP and latency
scopeHtml: Scope: switches vs routers, routing tables, BGP and internet structure, latency vs distance.

notes.title: Switch vs router vs hub
notes.html:
A switch connects devices inside one network using MAC addresses. A router connects different networks using IP addresses. A hub (obsolete) just repeats every bit to every port.

A switch learns: when a frame arrives on port 3 from MAC aa:bb, it records aa:bb -> port 3 in its MAC table. Later frames to aa:bb go only to port 3. Unknown destination or broadcast: flood out all other ports.

$ bridge fdb show br0       # Linux bridge MAC table
aa:bb:cc:00:00:01 dev eth1 master br0
aa:bb:cc:00:00:02 dev eth2 master br0

Worked example. A 48-port gigabit switch has a backplane of 96 Gbps (48 x 1 Gbps x 2 for full duplex) and can forward all ports at line rate. A hub would share 1 Gbps across everyone, with collisions.

Industry examples. Data center switches from Arista, Cisco and Juniper, and in-house ones by Google and Meta (white-box switches running SONiC). Home "routers" are really a router, switch, Wi-Fi AP, NAT and DHCP server in one box.

Everyday analogy. A switch is an office mail clerk who knows every desk; a router is the post office that sends letters between buildings.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a switch an L3 device. L2 switches forward by MAC; "L3 switches" also route in hardware.
  • Forgetting the MAC table is finite (a few thousand to 100k+ entries); MAC flooding fills it and turns the switch into a hub.

notes.title: VLANs and broadcast domains
notes.html:
A broadcast domain is every device that hears a broadcast (like ARP). A VLAN splits one physical switch into several isolated broadcast domains. Frames get a 4-byte 802.1Q tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID (1 to 4094). Access ports carry one VLAN untagged; trunk ports carry many tagged VLANs.

Different VLANs talk only through a router (inter-VLAN routing, "router on a stick" or an L3 switch SVI).

Worked example. 1,000 hosts on one flat L2 produce thousands of ARP and broadcast packets per second that every host must process. Splitting into four /24 VLANs of 250 hosts cuts broadcast load about 4x and limits the blast radius of a loop.

Industry examples. Cloud networks avoid VLAN limits (4,094) with VXLAN (24-bit VNI, 16M segments), used by AWS-like overlays, Kubernetes CNIs (Flannel, Calico VXLAN mode) and VMware NSX.

Decision gravity. Segmentation by VLAN is cheap and reversible, but stretching L2 across data centers is risky (loops, storms). Modern DCs route (L3) to the top-of-rack switch and overlay L2 on top where needed.

Everyday analogy. Floors of a building: a shout on floor 2 is not heard on floor 5; to talk across floors you use the lift (router).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing VLANs are security by themselves; misconfigured trunks allow VLAN hopping.
  • Not knowing spanning tree (STP) exists to stop L2 loops, which otherwise cause broadcast storms that take the network down in seconds.

notes.title: How a router decides: routing tables
notes.html:
A router holds a table of prefixes and picks the most specific match (longest prefix match). Each entry says "for destination X/n, send to next hop Y out of interface Z".

$ ip route
default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0
10.0.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.0.15
10.0.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.2 dev eth0
10.0.1.128/25 via 10.0.0.3 dev eth0

Packet to 10.0.1.200: matches 10.0.1.0/24 (24 bits) and 10.0.1.128/25 (25 bits, longer); the /25 wins, so next hop 10.0.0.3. Packet to 8.8.8.8 matches only default (0.0.0.0/0).

Routes arrive three ways: connected (the interface's own subnet), static (an admin typed it), dynamic (learned from protocols). When multiple sources offer the same prefix, administrative distance picks (connected 0, static 1, OSPF 110, RIP 120, eBGP 20 on Cisco-style devices).

Worked example. Core internet routers hold ~1 million IPv4 prefixes in specialised memory (TCAM); lookup happens in a few nanoseconds in hardware. Software routers use tries.

Industry examples. Cloud route tables (AWS VPC) work this way: 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-xxx makes a subnet public, -> nat-xxx makes it private, 10.1.0.0/16 -> pcx-xxx sends to a peered VPC; the most specific route wins.

Everyday analogy. A GPS-less driver following signs: "Mumbai" sign vs "Mumbai Andheri" sign: you follow the more specific one.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting longest prefix match and explaining by order of rules.
  • Missing the return route: a ping works one way, fails the other because the far side has no route back.
  • Asymmetric routing breaking stateful firewalls.

notes.title: Interior routing: OSPF, RIP and data center routing
notes.html:
Inside one organisation (an autonomous system), routers learn routes from each other by an interior gateway protocol (IGP).

  • RIP: distance-vector, counts hops (max 15). Simple, slow, obsolete.
  • OSPF: link-state; every router floods its links to all others, each runs Dijkstra to build the map. Fast convergence, scales to hundreds of routers in areas. Cost depends on bandwidth.
  • IS-IS: similar link-state, favoured by ISPs.
  • Data center fabrics: often eBGP in leaf-spine (Meta, Microsoft), since BGP handles huge scale and policy.

Worked example (convergence). A link fails. OSPF with default timers (hello 10 s, dead 40 s) takes up to 40 s to notice; with BFD (bidirectional forwarding detection) at 50 ms x 3 detection is ~150 ms. Tuning detection time is the main lever.

Industry examples. Calico can peer pods with the data center via BGP; Kubernetes pod routes advertised so no overlay is needed. Cilium offers BGP control plane too.

Decision gravity. Choosing a routing protocol is mostly a one-way door at the fabric level (changing it means a migration); for small networks static routes are simpler and fine.

Everyday analogy. Every taxi driver in a city sharing the live traffic map (link-state) versus asking neighbours "how far are you from the airport?" (distance vector).

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up "IGP inside an AS" and "BGP between ASes".
  • Forgetting that dynamic routing can loop briefly during convergence; the TTL field is the safety net.

notes.title: BGP: how the internet is stitched together
notes.html:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how autonomous systems tell each other which IP prefixes they can reach. Each AS has a number (ASN): Google 15169, Cloudflare 13335, AWS 16509 (AS14618 also). A router advertises "I can reach 8.8.8.0/24 via AS path [15169]"; neighbours prepend their own ASN and pass it on. The AS path is also loop protection (a router drops a route containing its own ASN).

BGP is a path-vector protocol that runs over TCP port 179, driven by policy (money and contracts), not shortest distance. Rough order of best path selection: highest local preference, shortest AS path, lowest origin type, lowest MED, eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost.

Relationships between ASes:

  • Customer to provider (transit): the customer pays for access to the whole internet.
  • Peer to peer: two ASes swap traffic for each other's customers free (at an Internet Exchange like AMS-IX, DE-CIX, NIXI in India).
  • Rule of thumb ("valley-free"): don't give free transit; ASes advertise customer routes to everybody, but peer and provider routes only to customers.
# Looking-glass style view of a route
$ whois -h whois.radb.net 8.8.8.0/24
route:   8.8.8.0/24
origin:  AS15169
$ birdc show route for 8.8.8.8 all     # on a BIRD router
8.8.8.0/24 via 198.51.100.2 [bgp 12:00] * (100) [AS15169i]
        BGP.as_path: 3356 15169

Worked example. Internet shape: about 75,000+ active ASNs and ~1 million IPv4 routes (2024 to 2025 figures; confirm current). A global router full table takes about 1 to 2 GB RAM on software routers.

Real incidents. (1) 2008: Pakistan Telecom announced a more specific YouTube prefix to block it locally and leaked it, blackholing YouTube worldwide for ~2 hours. (2) 2021: Facebook withdrew its prefixes during a bad maintenance command, so its DNS and services disappeared; internal tools also died. (3) 2019: a small ISP's route leak via Verizon took out chunks of Cloudflare and AWS traffic. Mitigations: RPKI route origin validation (ROAs), prefix filters, max-prefix limits, MANRS.

Decision gravity. Becoming multi-homed (two upstreams) buys resilience and is reversible per link; announcing your own prefixes needs an ASN and PI address space (a registry process, hard to undo). BGP has no built-in security; RPKI adoption is gradual.

Everyday analogy. Airlines code-sharing: each airline only tells partners where it flies; you choose by price and agreements, not the shortest flight.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying BGP picks the fastest route. It follows business policy and AS path length.
  • Forgetting eBGP vs iBGP; iBGP does not change the AS path.
  • Not knowing that more specific prefixes win, which is how hijacks work.

notes.title: The internet's structure: tiers, IXPs and CDNs
notes.html:
The internet is a loose hierarchy plus a lot of direct shortcuts.

  • Tier 1 networks (Lumen, Arelion, NTT, Tata Communications, etc.) can reach every route without paying anyone; they peer with each other.
  • Tier 2 / regional ISPs buy transit and also peer.
  • Access ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Comcast) serve homes and phones.
  • IXPs are switches where many networks connect and peer cheaply (DE-CIX in Frankfurt peaks above 14 Tbps).
  • Content networks (Google, Netflix, Meta, Akamai, Cloudflare) peer directly with access ISPs or place caches inside them, so most traffic never touches Tier 1 carriers.

Worked example (cost). Video from a faraway origin: transit costs maybe $0.50 to $2 per Mbps per month at scale. Netflix at 20 Tbps average would pay a fortune, so Open Connect boxes inside ISPs cut transit to near zero for 90%+ of its bytes.

Industry examples. Google's Espresso/Edge peering and its private subsea cables (Dunant, Equiano); Meta and Microsoft cable consortia. About 95%+ of international data crosses roughly 500+ submarine cables.

Decision gravity. Where you peer or place PoPs is a long-term contract choice. Using a cloud's backbone (e.g. AWS Global Accelerator, Cloudflare Argo) is rentable and reversible.

Everyday analogy. Highways (Tier 1), state roads (regional), local streets (access) and private expressways that big companies built to their own warehouses (content networks).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only a strict hierarchy; the flat peering model is what dominates today.
  • Not knowing what an IXP is.

notes.title: Latency vs distance
notes.html:
Latency is delay, bandwidth is capacity. Latency has a physical floor: light in fibre goes about 200 km per millisecond (about 5 microseconds per km). RTT floor = 2 x distance / 200 km per ms. Real RTTs are 1.5x to 2x that, because cables are not straight and routers add delay.

Route Great-circle distance Floor RTT Typical real RTT
Same city 20 km 0.2 ms 1 to 5 ms
Mumbai to Delhi 1,150 km 11.5 ms 20 to 30 ms
Mumbai to Singapore 3,900 km 39 ms 55 to 70 ms
Mumbai to Frankfurt 6,500 km 65 ms 110 to 130 ms
Mumbai to New York 12,500 km 125 ms 180 to 220 ms
Geostationary satellite 2 x 35,786 km up ~480 ms 600+ ms (Starlink LEO: 25 to 60 ms)

Latency components: propagation (distance/speed), transmission (size / bandwidth: 1,500 B at 10 Mbps = 1.2 ms), queuing (bufferbloat, can be hundreds of ms), processing (routers, TLS, app).

Worked example (bandwidth-delay product). 1 Gbps link with 100 ms RTT holds 1 Gbps x 0.1 s = 100 Mbit = 12.5 MB in flight. A TCP connection needs a window at least that large to fill the pipe; otherwise throughput = window / RTT. A 64 KB window at 100 ms RTT gives 64 KB / 0.1 s = 640 KB/s (about 5 Mbps) on a 1 Gbps link, which is why long fat networks need window scaling (see TCP notes).

Fixes ranked. (1) Move data closer: CDN, edge cache, regional DB replicas. (2) Fewer round trips: keep-alive, HTTP/2 or 3, batching, TLS 1.3 / 0-RTT, GraphQL or aggregated APIs. (3) Parallelise. (4) Compress to cut transfer time. You cannot buy a faster speed of light.

mtr -rwc 50 -n example.com          # see per-hop latency and loss
ping -c 10 -i 0.2 host              # jitter from mdev
curl -w "connect:%{time_connect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n" -so /dev/null https://host

Industry examples. Cloud multi-region design (DynamoDB global tables, Spanner) is a trade of consistency against cross-region RTT (US to EU ~80 to 100 ms). High-frequency traders pay millions for microwave links between Chicago and New Jersey (about 3.9 ms one way versus ~6.5 ms on fibre). WhatsApp and Cloudflare terminate TCP/TLS near users to shorten handshakes.

Everyday analogy. Water in a long pipe: wide pipe (bandwidth) lets lots flow at once, but the first drop still takes time to arrive (latency).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing bandwidth with latency: a faster plan does not reduce RTT.
  • Forgetting a request chain of N sequential calls over 100 ms RTT costs N x 100 ms (chatty APIs).
  • Quoting averages; p99 latency is what users feel.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Switches forward frames by MAC inside a network; routers forward packets by IP between networks, using longest prefix match.
  • VLANs and L3 boundaries limit broadcast domains; STP prevents L2 loops.
  • IGPs (OSPF, IS-IS) run inside an AS; BGP is the path-vector, policy-driven protocol between ASes over TCP 179.
  • BGP trust problems cause leaks and hijacks (YouTube 2008, Facebook 2021); RPKI and filters mitigate them.
  • The internet is flatter now: IXPs, direct peering and CDN caches inside ISPs.
  • Latency floor is about 1 ms RTT per 100 km of fibre; bandwidth-delay product decides window sizes; the main fix is moving data closer and cutting round trips.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a hub, a switch and a router?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic vocabulary for where traffic is flooded, forwarded or routed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A hub repeats every bit out of every port (one collision domain, obsolete). A switch learns which MAC lives on which port and forwards frames only there; it works at L2 inside one broadcast domain. A router forwards packets between networks by IP prefix and separates broadcast domains.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Switch MAC table:  aa:..:01 -> port 1 | aa:..:02 -> port 2
Unknown dest MAC   -> flood to all ports in the VLAN
Router: dst IP 10.2.3.4 -> longest prefix match -> next hop + egress interface

The switch learns by reading the source MAC of incoming frames, ageing entries (typically 300 s). Broadcasts (ARP, DHCP) flood to everyone in the VLAN. A router rewrites L2 headers per hop and decrements TTL. "L3 switches" do both in hardware (ASICs), which is why most data centers route at the top-of-rack.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking a switch understands IP.
  • Saying a router "connects computers" without naming broadcast domain separation.
  • Forgetting unknown-unicast flooding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the MAC table size limit effect? -> Overflow makes the switch flood like a hub (CAM attack).
  2. Where does a default gateway live? -> On a router or L3 interface of the VLAN.
  3. Why prefer routed access in the DC? -> Smaller failure domains, ECMP, no spanning tree.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the layers. Senior talks about broadcast domains, flooding behaviour and failure domains.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A giant flat L2 network collapsed under broadcast load from a single misbehaving host.

questions.promptHtml: What is a VLAN and a broadcast domain, and why split a network into VLANs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core to segmentation, security and scaling questions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive each other's L2 broadcasts. A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain carved out of physical switches by tagging frames with a 12-bit ID (802.1Q). VLANs reduce broadcast noise, isolate groups, and traffic between VLANs must go through a router.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Port 1-10: VLAN 10 (servers)    Port 11-20: VLAN 20 (guests)
Trunk link carries both: frame + 4-byte 802.1Q tag (VID 10 or 20)
VLAN 10 <-> VLAN 20 requires an L3 interface (SVI) / router

12 bits give 4094 usable VLANs; VXLAN (24-bit VNI, 16M segments) overlays L2 over L3 for large data centers. Each VLAN typically maps to one IP subnet. Isolation by VLAN alone is weaker than a firewall policy because misconfiguration (native VLAN, VLAN hopping) can leak.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating VLANs as security boundaries without ACLs.
  • Forgetting the trunk's allowed VLAN list.
  • Putting 5000 hosts in one VLAN.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Access vs trunk port? -> Access carries one untagged VLAN; trunk carries many tagged.
  2. What is the native VLAN? -> The untagged VLAN on a trunk; a hopping risk if misused.
  3. Why VXLAN? -> Beyond 4094 VLANs and to stretch L2 across a routed fabric.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "logical network". Senior: broadcast scaling, subnet-per-VLAN, trunking, VXLAN.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A new VLAN missing from a trunk's allowed list isolated half a rack.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you get Mumbai to Virginia round-trip latency under about 130 ms, and what contributes to real-world numbers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates physics you cannot beat from overhead you can.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Light in fibre travels at about 200,000 km/s, roughly 200 km per millisecond (two thirds of c). Mumbai to Virginia is about 13,000 km great-circle, so at least 65 ms one way and 130 ms RTT. Real cables are longer than the great-circle line, plus router hops, queuing and handshakes, so 180-250 ms is typical (verify with measurement).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RTT_min = 2 x distance / 200 km per ms.

Same city  50 km   -> 0.5 ms RTT
Cross-US 4,000 km  -> 40 ms
India-US east 13,000 km -> 130 ms floor

Components: propagation (physics), serialisation (size/bandwidth: 1500 B at 1 Gbps = 12 us), queuing (variable), processing. Bandwidth does not reduce propagation delay. Only moving data closer (CDN, regional deploy) or fewer round trips helps.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking more bandwidth fixes latency.
  • Using straight-line distance as the real path.
  • Ignoring multiple RTTs per request.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a satellite link slow? -> Geostationary orbit ~36,000 km up means ~500+ ms RTT; LEO (Starlink) tens of ms.
  2. How many ms of the budget does a TLS handshake cost? -> 1-2 RTT beyond TCP.
  3. Does hollow-core fibre help? -> Approximately 30% faster propagation (verify), niche.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "far means slow". Senior calculates the floor and counts the RTTs per user action.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cross-region DB call per request multiplied a 70 ms RTT by 30 queries, producing a 2 s page.

questions.contextHtml:
A Linux gateway has this table. Traffic to 10.50.3.40 is going out the wrong interface to the internet instead of through the VPN, and engineers insist "the VPN route is there":

$ ip route
default via 192.0.2.1 dev eth0 metric 100
10.50.0.0/16 dev tun0 scope link
10.50.3.0/24 via 192.0.2.77 dev eth0
192.0.2.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.0.2.10
$ ip route get 10.50.3.40
10.50.3.40 via 192.0.2.77 dev eth0 src 192.0.2.10

A teammate added the /24 last week for an urgent test.
questions.promptHtml: Why is this behaviour correct, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Routes are in the wrong order" or "metric is wrong." Routing is not first match by order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who added 10.50.3.0/24 and why? Is 192.0.2.77 meant to reach this network? Is the test finished?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the /24 route (ip route del 10.50.3.0/24 via 192.0.2.77) if it is not needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A more specific route is overriding; policy routing rule; the VPN route not installed (not here).
  4. How I'd verify each: ip route get <ip>, ip rule, ip route show table all.
  5. Root cause: Routers use longest prefix match: a /24 beats a /16 regardless of order or metric. Metric only breaks ties between equal-length prefixes.
  6. Fix: Delete the stray route, or if needed move 10.50.3.0/24 behind the VPN. Persist the removal in config management, because a manually added route disappears on reboot while a persisted one may return.
  7. Prevention: Route changes through code review; alert on unexpected more-specific routes; document owners.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not add a /25 to override the /24 (an arms race); do not tune metrics for this.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two /24 routes with different metrics? -> Lower metric wins; equal metric may ECMP.
  • What if tun0 goes down? -> The /16 vanishes and traffic falls to the default route, possibly leaking out.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A test route for one host lived for six months and sent a production subnet's backups over the public internet.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reorders routes.
  • Hire: explains longest prefix match and removes the route.
  • Strong hire: uses ip route get, handles leak risk on tunnel failure, and adds change control.

questions.promptHtml: What is BGP, how does a router pick between two paths to the same prefix, and why is it called trust-based?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: BGP outages and hijacks make news; the mechanism is common for cloud/CDN roles.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: BGP is the protocol between autonomous systems: each AS announces the prefixes it can reach with an AS_PATH of the networks it crosses. A router picks the best path by policy first (highest local-preference), then shortest AS_PATH, and other tie-breakers. It is trust based because by default a neighbour's announcement is believed; nothing proves the origin AS owns the prefix.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AS 64500 announces 203.0.113.0/24
   path seen by AS 64511: [64496, 64500]   (length 2)
   path via other peer:   [64499, 64498, 64500] (length 3)

Order (simplified): highest local-pref, shortest AS_PATH, lowest origin type, lowest MED, eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost. Business routing: customer routes preferred over peer over transit (it earns money). Defences: RPKI route origin validation (ROAs), IRR filters, max-prefix limits, MANRS. BGP converges slowly (tens of seconds to minutes) and a bad announcement spreads fast.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing BGP chooses the fastest path; it chooses by policy and path length.
  • Forgetting more-specific prefixes win before any attribute.
  • Thinking the cloud hides BGP from you (Direct Connect, VPNs use it).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. eBGP vs iBGP? -> Between ASes vs inside an AS; iBGP needs a full mesh or route reflectors.
  2. What is a route leak? -> Re-announcing routes to a neighbour who should not receive them, attracting traffic.
  3. How does RPKI help? -> Signed ROAs declare which AS may originate a prefix; routers drop invalid origins.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "routing between ISPs". Senior: policy first, longest prefix first, RPKI, convergence time and blast radius.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mistaken AS_PATH-prepend change shifted all traffic onto a more expensive transit link.

questions.contextHtml:
After a switch replacement, app servers in VLAN 20 (10.20.0.0/24) cannot reach DB servers in VLAN 30 (10.30.0.0/24). Both sets reach their own gateways. Config snippet from the new core switch:

interface Vlan20
 ip address 10.20.0.1 255.255.255.0
interface Vlan30
 ip address 10.30.0.1 255.255.255.0
 shutdown
!
interface Te1/1/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20

App server traceroute 10.30.0.15 shows hop 1 10.20.0.1 and then * * *. DB servers reach the internet through a different path.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you fix it with minimal blast radius?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reboot the switch." Misses the shutdown SVI and the trunk allowed list.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the old switch config copied exactly? Which port connects the DB-side switch? Is a change window available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: no shutdown on Vlan30 and add VLAN 30 to the trunk (switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: SVI for VLAN 30 down so no gateway; VLAN 30 missing from the trunk; VLAN not created in the VLAN database; ACL.
  4. How I'd verify each: show ip interface brief, show interfaces trunk, show vlan id 30, show ip route 10.30.0.0.
  5. Root cause: Inter-VLAN traffic needs an L3 interface per VLAN. Vlan30 is shut down, so the route to 10.30.0.0/24 doesn't exist, and VLAN 30 frames are not permitted across the trunk anyway.
  6. Fix: Both changes above. DB servers reaching the internet via a different path explains why only VLAN-to-VLAN broke.
  7. Prevention: Config diff review when replacing devices, pre/post-change reachability tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not use allowed vlan 30 without add (it would replace the list and cut VLANs 10 and 20); do not open a permit-any ACL.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did I say add? -> The command without add overwrites the allowed list, a classic outage.
  • Traffic works one way only? -> Check return route / asymmetric routing or stateful firewall.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A replacement switch took the whole cluster down for 20 minutes because the trunk allowed list was typed without the "add" keyword.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reboots.
  • Hire: finds the shutdown SVI and the trunk list.
  • Strong hire: uses the add keyword, verifies with show commands and builds diff-based change checks.

questions.contextHtml: Your service in Mumbai calls a payment API in Virginia, once per user action with 4 sequential calls (auth, risk, charge, confirm), each over a fresh connection (TCP + TLS 1.2). Measured RTT is 205 ms. Users complain about 3-4 s checkouts. The vendor is not moving. Budget for the whole flow: 1.5 s.
questions.promptHtml: Compute where time goes and how you reach the target.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a faster server." Never multiplies RTTs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the 4 calls dependent? Can they be batched? Does the vendor support HTTP/2 or keep-alive? Is there a regional endpoint?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reuse connections (keep-alive pool) and parallelise independent calls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Handshake overhead per call, sequential chain, TLS version, no connection pooling.
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -w timing from Mumbai for connect/TLS/TTFB; check client pool settings.
  5. Root cause (math): Per call on a fresh connection: TCP 1 RTT + TLS 1.2 2 RTT + request 1 RTT = 4 RTT = 820 ms. Four calls = 3.28 s. That matches the complaint; server time is small.
  6. Fix: Warm pool: each call costs 1 RTT = 205 ms, 4 calls = 820 ms. TLS 1.3 saves one more RTT for the first call. Run risk and auth in parallel: critical path 3 calls = 615 ms. Or place a small relay in us-east that makes the 4 calls locally (1 RTT from Mumbai plus ~5 ms) - total about 250 ms.
  7. Prevention: Latency budget per dependency in design docs; synthetic checks by region.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A relay adds a component with security and compliance implications (it handles payment data). Parallelism changes failure semantics; retries need idempotency keys.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vendor only supports HTTP/1.1 with 60 s idle close? -> Keep pool warm with periodic requests, size pool for concurrency.
  • Cannot relay for compliance? -> Co-locate the whole checkout nearer the vendor.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching a cross-ocean client from new-connection-per-call to a pool cut a checkout from 3.4 s to 0.9 s with no vendor change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale compute.
  • Hire: counts RTTs and adds pooling.
  • Strong hire: parallelises, considers relay trade-offs and idempotency.

questions.promptHtml: Compare OSPF, RIP and BGP, and explain why many data centers now run BGP (or similar) inside the fabric.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows understanding of routing protocol families and DC design trends.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: RIP is distance-vector by hop count, slow and capped at 15 hops, so obsolete. OSPF is link-state: every router floods topology, runs Dijkstra and finds the shortest path by cost; fast convergence, good inside one organisation. BGP is policy-based path-vector for between (and now within) networks. Large DCs use eBGP per rack/switch because it scales, is simple to debug, offers policy control and avoids flooding the link-state database.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RIP  : tells neighbours its table every 30 s; hop count; max 15
OSPF : areas; LSAs flood; SPF per router; convergence ~ sub-second to seconds
BGP  : TCP session between neighbours; incremental updates; policy

In a Clos (leaf-spine) fabric every leaf connects to every spine; each switch is its own AS (or ASN per tier), eBGP over point-to-point /31s, ECMP across spines. A failure only withdraws affected prefixes; no area design needed.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying OSPF is for the internet.
  • Assuming BGP is only external.
  • Ignoring convergence time implications.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why /31 links? -> Saves addresses; 2 usable on point-to-point links (RFC 3021).
  2. What is BFD? -> Fast failure detection (sub-second) so routing reacts quickly.
  3. What are OSPF areas for? -> Limit flooding scope and SPF recomputation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "OSPF inside, BGP outside". Senior explains Clos fabrics with eBGP+ECMP and BFD.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky link without BFD took 40 s to be declared dead, black-holing traffic meanwhile.

questions.contextHtml:
A service behind four equal-cost paths shows one 10 Gbps uplink at 95% (drops) while the other three sit at 20%. Traffic is mostly large backups between two hosts using a single TCP connection per transfer, and a handful of elephant flows. Route table:

10.9.0.0/16 proto bgp metric 20
        nexthop via 10.0.1.1 dev eth1 weight 1
        nexthop via 10.0.2.1 dev eth2 weight 1
        nexthop via 10.0.3.1 dev eth3 weight 1
        nexthop via 10.0.4.1 dev eth4 weight 1

ip -s link shows eth2 with growing TX drops. Total demand is about 18 Gbps over 40 Gbps capacity.
questions.promptHtml: Why is ECMP not balancing, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ECMP is broken; add a fifth path." The hashing is working as designed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many flows exist? Are flows long-lived? Which hash fields (L3 only or L4)? Are the senders using one TCP connection?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Split the backup into several parallel streams (multi-connection) so hashing spreads them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Few elephant flows collide on one link via hash; hash uses only src/dst IP so all traffic between two hosts is one flow; polarisation (same hash at multiple tiers).
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-flow stats (ss -ti, flow telemetry/sFlow/NetFlow), ip route get 10.9.1.5 from 10.8.0.5 ipproto tcp sport 40000 dport 873 with varying ports, and sysctl net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy.
  5. Root cause: ECMP hashes the 5-tuple to keep a flow on one path (preserving packet order). With few big flows, hash assigns by flow, not by bytes, so the distribution is lumpy; one link got two elephants.
  6. Fix: Short term: multiple connections per transfer; set hash policy to include L4 ports (fib_multipath_hash_policy=1). Long term: flowlet/adaptive load balancing, or per-packet spraying with reordering-tolerant transport; traffic engineering for elephants.
  7. Prevention: Monitor per-link utilisation variance; capacity plan to at most 50% on any single link given the hash imbalance.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Per-packet balancing causes reordering that hurts TCP. Not add equal-cost paths without fixing flow counts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does one flow stay on one path? -> Reordering across paths with different delays triggers false fast retransmits.
  • Uneven link speeds in ECMP? -> Use weights (UCMP).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A replication job opened one connection and pinned 9 Gbps on a single uplink; splitting it into 8 streams removed the drops without any hardware.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames hardware.
  • Hire: explains 5-tuple hashing and elephant flows.
  • Strong hire: verifies the hash policy, proposes multi-stream and discusses reordering trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
At 14:02 your API (AS 64500, prefix 198.51.100.0/22) becomes unreachable from several ISPs; others fine. Your monitoring shows traffic fell 40%. A looking-glass query reveals:

198.51.100.0/24  path: 65010 64999 64777   <- origin AS 64777, not you
198.51.100.0/22  path: 65010 64500

Your NOC has no BGP expertise on call tonight. AS 64777 is a small ISP in another continent. Your /22 is covered by a ROA authorising 64500 with maxLength 22.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and what do you do in the first hour and after?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call the cloud provider and wait." Doesn't realise a more-specific /24 beats your /22.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which ISPs are affected? Is the /24 announcement still visible? Do we have emergency contacts for our transit providers and the origin ISP? Do we have any pre-signed ROAs and prepared /24 announcements?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Announce the more-specific /24s of our own (198.51.100.0/24 through 198.51.103.0/24) from our AS to win longest-prefix match; ask transit providers to filter the bogus origin.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hijack (malicious) or leak/misconfiguration (a customer of 64777 originating our prefix by mistake). Both look identical from routing; intent comes later.
  4. How I'd verify each: Looking glass / RIPE RIS / bgp.tools for the origin and propagation; check RPKI status (invalid origin and also invalid by maxLength).
  5. Root cause: BGP prefers the most specific prefix before any attribute. 64777's /24 attracts traffic from every network that accepts it. Networks doing RPKI origin validation reject it; those that don't accept it.
  6. Fix: Short term: announce /24s (valid under ROA? maxLength 22 would make our /24s RPKI invalid, so pre-update the ROA to maxLength 24, or contact upstreams to filter). Contact 64777's NOC and their upstream to withdraw. Long term: sign ROAs with proper maxLength strategy, monitor with BGP alerting (e.g. origin change alerts), contract transit providers that enforce RPKI/IRR filtering.
  7. Prevention: RPKI ROAs, BGP monitoring with alerts, tested runbook for emergency de-aggregation, MANRS membership.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: De-aggregation bloats the global table and should be temporary; a /24 is generally the smallest accepted. Do not withdraw our own /22.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not simply set maxLength 24 permanently? -> It permits a hijacker to originate /24 forged paths with our ASN (forged-origin attacks) because ROV only checks origin; tradeoff to evaluate.
  • Traffic is already flowing to the hijacker; what about data exposure? -> Treat as potential interception; TLS and certificate pinning limit damage; rotate secrets if sensitive plaintext traffic was exposed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A small ISP typo leaked a global prefix for roughly an hour; the impacted company recovered faster because it had a pre-written runbook and a contact at the right transit provider.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits for the ISP.
  • Hire: recognises longest-prefix hijack and de-aggregates.
  • Strong hire: reasons about RPKI maxLength, contacts upstreams, plans monitoring and preparation.

questions.contextHtml: You serve a global API (30% US, 25% EU, 30% India/SEA, 15% LATAM) from three regions. Static assets are already on a CDN. API p95 TTFB from India is 520 ms vs 140 ms in the US. Each API call is dynamic and user-specific; writes are strongly consistent in us-east. The CFO wants a plan under $20k/month extra. Anycast is available from your CDN vendor.
questions.promptHtml: Design the improvement, including what anycast does and doesn't give you.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Put everything on the CDN." Dynamic, personalised writes can't just be cached.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share is read vs write? How stale can reads be? Which endpoints are on the critical path? What are the data residency rules?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable CDN as a reverse proxy for the API (edge TLS termination, persistent connections to origin).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Handshake RTT from India to Virginia dominates (~3-4 RTTs); cross-ocean path quality; origin-side DB cross-region calls.
  4. How I'd verify each: RUM by region with timing split, compare edge TTFB to origin TTFB (cf-cache-status/server-timing), traceroute from probes.
  5. Root cause: Distance and handshake count; anycast routes a user to the nearest edge by BGP (hop count/policy, not latency), but the edge still has to reach the origin for uncached dynamic calls.
  6. Fix: Phase 1: anycast edge termination + warm pooled connections to origin (handshake becomes ~20 ms; remaining one origin RTT ~210 ms), giving about 300 ms. Phase 2: cache GET responses with short TTL and stale-while-revalidate for safe endpoints. Phase 3: a read replica in ap-south and route reads locally, writes to primary; session stickiness for read-your-writes.
  7. Prevention: Per-region SLOs, synthetic probes, capacity and cost dashboards.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Multi-region writes (active-active) is expensive and complex; avoid it until read-local isn't enough. Anycast can send users to a distant edge because BGP does not measure latency, and route flaps can break long TCP sessions to a different edge.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Anycast and TCP? -> A route change mid-connection sends packets to another edge that has no state and resets; mitigated by short connections/QUIC connection IDs and stable routing.
  • Why not DNS-based geo routing? -> Depends on resolver location (ECS support) and TTLs; coarser and slower to react.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Adding edge termination alone took an Asia API from 520 ms to 310 ms and made the read-replica project optional for another year.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "CDN for everything".
  • Hire: separates static from dynamic and uses edge termination.
  • Strong hire: understands anycast limits, stages cost-bounded steps and handles consistency.

questions.promptHtml: Describe a leaf-spine (Clos) data center network. What happens when a spine fails, and how do you size oversubscription?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests design thinking about capacity, redundancy and failure domains for large systems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every leaf (top-of-rack) switch connects to every spine switch. Any two servers in different racks are exactly leaf-spine-leaf, 2 hops apart, with N equal-cost paths. If a spine fails, routing withdraws it and traffic spreads over the remaining spines, losing 1/N of the bisection bandwidth. Oversubscription is downlink capacity to servers divided by uplink capacity to spines.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Spine1  Spine2  Spine3  Spine4
          |  \  /  |  \  /  |  \  /  |
Leaf1  ---+--------+--------+--------+
Leaf2  ---+--------+--------+--------+   (each leaf links to all spines)

Example: a leaf with 48 x 25G server ports (1200 G down) and 4 x 100G uplinks (400 G up) is 3:1 oversubscribed. With 4 spines, losing one cuts uplink to 300 G (4:1) while still working. Scale by adding spines (bandwidth) or pods via super-spines. Each flow is hashed to one path (ECMP), so uneven flow sizes still cause hot links. BFD gives sub-second failure detection.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting failure-mode capacity (plan for N-1).
  • Assuming uniform load distribution.
  • Mixing L2 stretch with the fabric, bringing back spanning tree.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not a three-tier tree? -> Core links become bottlenecks and have STP blocked paths.
  2. East-west vs north-south traffic? -> Modern services produce more east-west, which Clos suits.
  3. How to scale beyond one pod? -> Add a super-spine tier (5-stage Clos).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "leaf connects to spines". Senior computes oversubscription, N-1 behaviour and ECMP hot spots.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fabric designed at 3:1 became 4.5:1 after a spine maintenance window plus a failure, saturating storage replication traffic.

questions.contextHtml:
At 11:12 an entire office floor loses connectivity. Switch CPU is at 99%, every access port's LED is flashing, and the MAC table shows the same MACs flapping between ports:

%SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF: Host 0050.56ab.cd01 in vlan 10 is flapping between port Gi1/0/5 and port Gi1/0/9
Interface Gi1/0/5: input rate 940 Mbps, 1.4M pps broadcasts

Someone had just plugged a small unmanaged 5-port switch under a desk, and connected two of its ports to two wall jacks. STP is off on the access ports "to speed up link-up (PortFast)". BPDU Guard is not configured.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, restore service, and prevent a repeat.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reboot the switch." The loop reappears immediately.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which ports are flapping? Any recent physical changes? Is STP enabled on the core?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Find the loop ports (flapping MAC and highest broadcast counters) and shut them or unplug the desk switch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Physical loop via rogue switch; misconfigured link aggregation; STP failure/misconfig. Red herring: a "DDoS" from the internet.
  4. How I'd verify each: show mac address-table flaps, show interfaces counters, show spanning-tree, port LED, ask who has plugged anything.
  5. Root cause: Layer 2 frames have no TTL. A broadcast entering a loop is copied around forever and multiplied at each switch, saturating links and CPU (a broadcast storm). Spanning tree would have blocked a port, but it was not active on these edge ports.
  6. Fix: Remove the loop, then enable BPDU Guard (err-disable on BPDU received on PortFast ports), storm-control on access ports, root guard, and keep STP running.
  7. Prevention: Edge policy templates (PortFast + BPDU Guard), storm-control thresholds (e.g. 1% broadcast), loop-guard, monitoring MAC flap logs, and routed access where possible.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not disable STP globally; storm-control may drop legitimate bursts (tune it).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does CPU hit 99%? -> Broadcasts are punted to the control plane (ARP, etc.) and the MAC table churns.
  • How does routed access avoid this? -> L3 boundaries stop floods; TTL kills loops.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A conference-room switch with two cables to one wall plate stalled a building for 40 minutes; BPDU Guard was in the standard template but not applied to that stack.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reboots.
  • Hire: spots the loop and removes it.
  • Strong hire: explains no-TTL amplification, adds BPDU Guard and storm-control, and proposes routed access.

questions.contextHtml: A monolith in eu-west reads from a Postgres primary in eu-west. A new feature in a us-east service executes 25 sequential SQL queries per request against that primary over a VPN. Measured inter-region RTT is 82 ms. Request p50 jumped from 90 ms to 2.4 s. Bandwidth use is trivial (5 Mbps). DB CPU is 8%. The team plans to "upgrade the VPN to 10 Gbps".
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the plan and propose a better one.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to upgrade bandwidth. Latency, not throughput, is the constraint.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can queries be batched? Are the reads cacheable? What consistency does the feature need? Could the service run in eu-west?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce round trips: batch queries (joins, IN, pipelining) and add a short-TTL cache.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N+1 query pattern times RTT; chatty ORM; no connection pool so each request pays connection setup; TLS per call.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query log with counts per request, pg_stat_statements, timing: 25 x 82 ms = 2.05 s plus connect and processing ~ 2.4 s.
  5. Root cause: Round trips times RTT: 25 sequential queries cost 25 x 82 = 2,050 ms regardless of link speed. A 10 Gbps pipe does not change propagation delay.
  6. Fix: Rewrite to 2-3 queries (joins), pipeline/prepared batches, or move the service to eu-west. If cross-region reads are inevitable, deploy a read replica in us-east (lag a few hundred ms acceptable?) and send only writes cross-region.
  7. Prevention: Per-request budget for cross-region calls; tests that count queries; tracing with spans showing sequential remote calls.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A replica brings replication lag and read-after-write issues (route recent-writer sessions to primary). Not buy bandwidth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just raise the VPN to a direct link? -> Reduces jitter maybe, but physics stays ~80 ms.
  • Writes still cross the region; fine? -> One write per request costs one RTT; acceptable if batched.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An ORM's lazy loading produced 120 queries on a profile page; moving the app next to the DB gave a 30x improvement without code changes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves bandwidth purchase.
  • Hire: multiplies queries by RTT.
  • Strong hire: proposes batching, replica, placement, and covers consistency effects.
